title: When unsafe AI becomes normal
originalTitle: The Normalization of Deviance in AI
deck: Small shortcuts can become standard practice when repeated success hides the risk.
takeaways: A successful run does not establish that an AI workflow is secure.
Treat model output as untrusted input before it reaches consequential actions.
Retain oversight and enforce permissions outside the model.

sections.heading: Trust needs a boundary
paragraphs: The author argues that probabilistic model responses need downstream access checks, encoding and sanitization. Model cooperation cannot replace these controls.

sections.heading: Success can conceal drift
paragraphs: Temporary shortcuts become routine when nothing visibly breaks. Competitive pressure makes teams more likely to forget why safeguards existed.

sections.heading: Two routes to harm
paragraphs: Overconfidence can amplify ordinary model mistakes. Attackers can exploit the same permissive workflow through malicious inputs or compromised models.

sections.heading: Make safeguards concrete
paragraphs: The essay recommends human leadership in sensitive workflows, alongside sandboxing, limited permissions and short-lived credentials.

interaction.title: Watch the baseline drift
interaction.label: An illustrative example · authored by researchx
interaction.description: Move through four fictional deployments of an assistant that can delete files. Each uneventful run tempts the team to remove a control. Compare the current safeguards with the original baseline. This conceptual illustration contains no measured failure rates.

steps.label: Initial rollout
steps.change: The assistant can suggest a deletion; a person executes it.

steps.label: One successful pilot
steps.change: The assistant receives write access after one quiet pilot.

steps.label: A busy release
steps.change: Approval is skipped to save time.

steps.label: Shortcut becomes policy
steps.change: The assistant is moved into the live workspace with unrestricted deletion.
